def: The act of selecting one of several alternatives, an expression of the freedom and autonomy of the one who chooses.
com: Having the freedom to choose does not say whether the choice is just: when there is a victim, the choice no longer concerns only the person making it. See Decision, Autonomy and Freedom.

def: The argument that a choice that concerns only the person making it should not be criticized or banned.
com: Veganism answers that eating animals affects a third party, the animal, so it stops being only a personal choice. The guide addresses the argument in chapter E1.

def: The cultivation of plants, such as grains, legumes, fruit and fibers, for human food, animal feed or other uses.
com: Veganism does not oppose agriculture, but the exploitation of animals. Part of agriculture serves to feed animals raised for consumption, and crop production also has impacts that deserve attention.

def: The combination of crop farming and livestock farming, that is, growing plants and raising animals.
com: The term joins two distinct activities, and veganism treats each differently: it opposes raising and using animals, but not growing plants.

def: A social and political movement that defends the protection of the environment, through laws, campaigns, parties and organizations.
com: It can have an anthropocentric, holistic or sentientist basis, depending on what it considers valuable in itself. See Environmentalism (moral).

def: An environmentalist view that gives moral value to the whole, such as ecosystems, species and the biotic community, and not to each individual.
com: Being consistent, it may accept sacrificing individuals, including humans, for the sake of the whole, a consequence Tom Regan called "environmental fascism". Its names include Aldo Leopold and J. Baird Callicott. It is close to ecocentrism.

def: An environmentalist view that protects the environment because it matters to human beings, which gives it instrumental value.
com: It already recognizes that individuals matter, people, so it has to explain why it would leave out the other animals who also feel.

def: A view that protects the environment because of the sentient beings who depend on it, human or not.
com: It keeps the individual at the center: when an environmental goal conflicts with the interests of beings who feel, what weighs is what happens to those who feel. The chapter on the divergence over ends in the Questão de Ética collection discusses the difference between animal defense and environmentalism that values species and ecosystems.

def: The same as a companion domestic animal, such as dogs and cats.
com: In Brazil the English word is widely used, including in shops and services. Some people prefer "companion animal" and "guardian" to "pet" and "owner", to mark that the animal is an individual and not property.

def: A structure, usually of metal, used in livestock farming to immobilize the animal, mainly cattle, during procedures such as vaccination, exams, treatments and insemination.
com: Activists call the structure used to immobilize females for forced insemination a "rape rack". See Brete.

def: A narrow, fenced corridor through which animals pass in single file, in livestock farming, to the restraint chute, the scale or loading.
com: Producers use "brete" and "tronco de contenção" for the set of handling structures. Activists call the restraint structure used in forced insemination a "rape rack".

def: The same as sentientism.
com: On this site the preferred term is sentientism. See Sentientism.

def: A current that joins veganism with anarchism and sees animal exploitation as a form of domination to be abolished along with the others.
com: The term was coined by Brian A. Dominick in 1995, in the text "Animal Liberation and Social Revolution".

def: A current that argues for ending animal exploitation within liberal democracy and the market economy, through rights, laws, consumer choices and innovation.
com: It is not an established label. Authors such as Alasdair Cochrane, Martha Nussbaum, Sue Donaldson and Will Kymlicka defend animals from liberal theory.

def: A current that links animal liberation to that of people with disabilities and criticizes the use of cognitive ability as a measure of worth.
com: Sunaura Taylor, in Beasts of Burden (2017), is a reference.

def: A position that sees technology, such as plant-based meat, cultivated meat and precision fermentation, as the fastest route to ending large-scale animal exploitation.
com: It is not an established label: the name describes a position that exists. Jacy Reese Anthis, in The End of Animal Farming (2018), and the Good Food Institute are examples.

def: An approach that chooses foundations and strategies by reason and by the best available evidence on what most reduces suffering and exploitation, with a willingness to revise positions.
com: It is not an established label. It works as a meta-strategy: it does not pick a side in advance, but a way of deciding. It is the approach of this guide.

def: Veganism or vegetarianism motivated by a religious tradition that asks for compassion and nonviolence toward animals, such as ahimsa in Jainism, Hinduism and Buddhism.
com: It includes Christian, Jewish and Muslim groups that argue for care for animals. It is veganism in the strict sense only when the reason includes animals and the refusal to exploit them.

def: A fallacy that tries to dismiss an argument by pointing out an inconsistency in whoever makes it, instead of examining the argument.
com: It is common in charges of hypocrisy against vegans: even if the charge is true, it does not change what happens to animals.

def: Presenting the strongest and most honest version of an argument before answering it, the opposite of the straw man.
com: It is the guide's method: each chapter presents the strongest version of the objection, shows what it gets right and only then where it fails.

def: A method of applying the same scenario or reasoning to human beings to see whether the answer would be accepted; if it would not, the reasoning may reveal speciesism.
com: It compares the structure of arguments, not the victims, and is used in every chapter of the guide.

def: An argument that discusses health, the environment, the economy, practicality or who defends veganism, rather than whether animals deserve respect.
com: It helps correct facts but does not settle the moral question on its own, and the answer to it is indirect too. Often it supports, at most, vegetarianism, eating less or environmentalism.

def: An argument that challenges the moral core: whether animals feel, whether the individual animal counts and whether using or killing it is wrong.
com: It is the ground on which the ethical question about animals is decided.

def: An estimate of how well or badly a being's life can go, from the worst to the best possible experience, compared with that of other beings.
com: It is not a moral weight by itself, and the estimates for insects and other invertebrates are provisional. The Moral Weight Project, from Rethink Priorities, is the reference.

def: The view that the lives of animals in nature are, in general, good and happy, in balance and free of significant suffering.
com: It is the popular and default view, supported by skewed images: large, charismatic animals appear far more often on covers and in documentaries than most wild animals, which are invertebrates and have many offspring, almost all dying early. Oscar Horta and Animal Ethics criticize this view. See Welfare biology.

def: A concept from the author Carol J. Adams: the animal who became food is made absent from the plate, by words and packaging that hide that there was a living individual and a death.
com: Words like "steak" and "chicken" separate the food from the animal. Rebuilding the link between what we eat and who was killed is a common awareness strategy. See The Sexual Politics of Meat (1990).

def: a form of substratism that gives less weight to the good of a sentient being because its body is not organic, carbon-based.
com: It stands to substratism as anthropocentrism stands to speciesism: the particular case that privileges one's own group. If what matters is the capacity to be harmed or benefited, the material the body is made of decides nothing. See Substratism, Speciesism and Sentience in AI and digital systems.

def: giving different weight to the good of a sentient being according to the substrate its body is made of, biological or digital, for example.
com: The parallel is direct: just as speciesism uses species as the criterion, and species says nothing about the capacity to suffer, substratism uses the material of the body, which says nothing either. The legitimate question is a different, empirical one: is that being sentient? See Carbonism, Speciesism and Sentience in robots.

def: the tendency to give more weight to what is near in time, treating future suffering as less important merely for being future; the position that adopts it as a principle is called temporalism.
com: The parallel is with distance in space: someone's pain ten thousand kilometres away is no smaller for it. Parfit distinguished discounting for uncertainty, which is legitimate, from pure discounting, merely for being later. See Impartiality, Temporal impartiality and Longtermism.

def: unbiased consideration of those affected by our decisions, whatever time they exist in.
com: It is impartiality applied to time, as spatial impartiality is applied to distance. Accepting it while excluding future animals adds two kinds of neglect together: temporal bias and speciesism. See Temporal bias and Longtermism.

def: conflict within a single movement, between people or currents that defend the same cause, when the dispute comes to consume more energy than the struggle for the shared goal.
com: Disagreeing about strategy is normal and can be useful, because it forces each side to show evidence. The problem begins when disagreement turns into personal attacks, purity tests and exclusion, which push away people who might join and help no animal. The End Infighting project gathers guidance on reducing these conflicts in the animal movement. See Abolitionism, Reformism and Institutional activism.

def: A diet without any animal products: no meat, fish, seafood, dairy, eggs or honey. It is the dietary part of veganism, which also rejects animal exploitation in clothing, entertainment and other uses.
com: Well planned, it is considered adequate at all stages of life by bodies such as the US Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, with vitamin B12 supplementation. People who follow it for health, without the ethical motivation, often use the term plant-based. See Veganism and Plant-based.

def: A fad diet that excludes all or almost all plant foods and is based on meat, eggs and sometimes dairy.
com: It is promoted on social media with stories of improved health, but there are no long-term studies of its safety. The main survey, from 2021, heard from 2,029 followers online, with self-reported data, and the authors urged caution; many participants had high LDL cholesterol. The diet excludes fiber and several plant nutrients. Not to be confused with carnism. See Carnivorism.

def: An ecological relationship in which one animal, the predator, kills and eats another, the prey.
com: It is one of the main causes of suffering and death of animals in the wild. Recognizing this does not mean advocating killing predators, which would make prey populations grow and increase hunger and disease; the discussion about reducing the suffering caused by predation is about the distant future and calls for research before any intervention. See Wild animal suffering and Parasitism.

def: An ecological relationship in which one organism, the parasite, lives in or on another, the host, and feeds on it, harming it, usually without killing it right away.
com: It is one of the most common ways of life in nature and a huge cause of suffering: worms, ticks and parasitoid wasp larvae, which eat the host alive from the inside, affect most wild animals. Recognizing this suffering is not defending parasitism or proposing to eradicate it now; it is asking how to help where it is already possible, as in treating injured or sick animals. See Predation and Wild animal suffering.

def: A vegan diet that includes bivalve molluscs, such as oysters, mussels and clams.
com: Its defenders argue that bivalves are probably not sentient, because they have no centralized brain, and that farming them causes little environmental harm. Science doesn't yet have a firm answer: scallops, for example, have dozens of eyes and swim to escape predators. So many vegans apply the precautionary principle and don't eat bivalves. The Vegan Society's definition of veganism excludes all animals, including bivalves. See Sentience and Veganism.

def: In biology, a diet based mainly on insects and other small invertebrates, characteristic of animals such as anteaters, many bats, swallows and geckos; applied to humans, eating insects, also called entomophagy.
com: Eating insects is traditional in several cultures, and insect farming has been promoted as a source of sustainable protein, for human consumption and mainly for animal feed. Since there is evidence that some insects may be sentient, and they are farmed and killed by the billions, the practice raises the same ethical questions as other animal farming. See Sentience and Carnivorism.

def: What is felt from the point of view of the one living through something: there being "something it is like to be" that being, in the words of the philosopher Thomas Nagel.
com: It is what distinguishes a sentient being from an object or a system that only reacts to stimuli: a stone has no experience, and a dog does. Sentience is the capacity to have good or bad subjective experiences, which is why it is the guide's moral criterion. The 2024 New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness states that there is strong scientific support for conscious experience in mammals and birds, and a realistic possibility in all vertebrates and many invertebrates, such as octopuses, crabs and insects. See Consciousness, Subjectivity and Sentience.

def: A systematic tendency of thought that distorts judgment in a predictable way, usually without the person noticing.
com: Biases aren't stupidity or bad faith: everyone has them, because the brain uses shortcuts. Some come up a lot in conversations about animals, such as confirmation bias, status quo bias and the cognitive dissonance of the meat paradox, which leads people to think the animals we eat feel less. Knowing your own biases helps you talk more honestly. The guide has a page with the most common biases about animals. See Fallacies and Cognitive dissonance.

def: Aversion to, distrust of or contempt for humanity in general.
com: It can appear in people who live with the injustice done to animals and conclude that humans are the problem. But misanthropy pushes away exactly the people who would need to change, and forgets that only humans have moral agency: only they can recognize the suffering of other beings and act to reduce it. The guide covers this in "Stop saying", under "If humans disappeared, the planet and the animals would be better off". See Activist burnout.

def: The existential anguish of being vegan in a world that normalizes animal exploitation: constant awareness of that exploitation, isolation and frustration at seeing that most people don't notice it.
com: The term was coined by the Australian psychologist Clare Mann in her book *Vystopia: The Anguish of Being Vegan in a Non-Vegan World* (2018). It is not a clinical diagnosis: the author describes it as an understandable response to what one knows about animals. The prevalence figures in circulation come from the author's own surveys. See Activist burnout and Vicarious trauma.

def: Physical, emotional and mental exhaustion in people devoted to a cause, leading to loss of energy, cynicism and often to leaving activism.
com: A study of social justice and human rights activists (Chen and Gorski, 2015) pointed to common causes such as neglecting self-care, the emotional weight of the cause and conflict among activists. In animal advocacy, frequent exposure to images of suffering and the feeling that change is slow add to this. The World Health Organization treats burnout as a work-related phenomenon, not as a disease. Looking after yourself is part of sustaining activism over the long term. See Activist fatigue, Vicarious trauma and Learned helplessness.

def: Accumulated tiredness in people who take part in campaigns, debates and actions for a long time, with falling motivation and energy.
com: It is milder and more common than burnout, but can lead to it without rest. A related concept is compassion fatigue, described among professionals who care for people in distress: the capacity to care diminishes after long exposure to others' pain. Breaks, support from others and realistic goals help prevent it. See Activist burnout.

def: Psychological distress in people who are repeatedly exposed to other people's trauma, even without having lived through it directly.
com: The concepts were first described among therapists and emergency workers: vicarious trauma by McCann and Pearlman (1990), secondary traumatic stress by Charles Figley. In animal advocacy, it mainly affects people who investigate or frequently watch footage of slaughter and abuse, and those who work in rescues and sanctuaries. It can bring intrusive thoughts, insomnia, irritability and avoidance. Limiting exposure and seeking support, including professional help, helps. See Activist burnout and Vystopia.

def: A state in which a person stops trying to change a situation because they have come to believe that nothing they do will make a difference.
com: The concept comes from experiments by Martin Seligman and Steven Maier in the 1960s with dogs given electric shocks, an example of the very animal suffering the guide discusses. In 2016, the same authors revised the theory: passivity in the face of pain would be the default response, and what is learned is the perception of control. In activism, it shows up as the feeling that exploitation is too big to change. Seeing concrete results, even small ones, helps get out of it. See Activist burnout and the argument "One person doesn't make a difference".

def: Something that happens or is the case, and that can be checked by observation or evidence.
com: Facts alone don't decide what we should do: from the fact that we have eaten meat for millennia it doesn't follow that we should keep doing so (see Hume's law on the fallacies page). But moral arguments depend on getting the facts right. "Fish don't feel pain" is a factual claim, and it can be checked. Telling apart fact, opinion and value helps you know what kind of answer each claim calls for. See Opinion and Truth.

def: A personal judgment about something, which may or may not be supported by reasons and evidence.
com: "That's my opinion" doesn't end the conversation. Opinions about facts can be checked, and moral opinions can be assessed by the reasons behind them and by their consistency with what the person already accepts. Everyone has the right to hold opinions, but not every opinion is equally well grounded. See Fact and the argument "Veganism is opinion, not science".

def: Correspondence between a statement and reality: a statement is true when things are as it says.
com: Factual statements are true or false regardless of who defends them. In ethics, philosophers debate whether moral judgments can also be true, the debate between moral realism and anti-realism. The guide doesn't depend on settling that question: it asks for consistency. If a human being's pain matters because it is pain, another sentient being's pain matters too. See Moral relativism, Fact and Opinion.

def: A widely held belief that isn't supported by the facts; in anthropology, also a traditional narrative that gives meaning to a culture, without necessarily being false.
com: In the debate about animals, a myth is a widespread false belief, such as "plant protein is incomplete" or "fish don't feel pain". But calling something a myth requires showing the evidence: a belief doesn't become a myth just because we disagree with it, and vegans repeat myths too, such as some exaggerations about health (see "Stop saying"). See Fact and Truth.

def: A reason given to show that an action or a belief is right.
com: In ethics, anyone who causes harm to someone needs a justification, and the guide examines precisely the justifications given for using animals. A good justification has to be factually true and morally relevant. It is also different from an explanation: explaining why someone does something, such as habit or culture, doesn't show that it is right to do it. See Argument and Fallacies.

def: The idea, set out by Charles Darwin, that the mental differences between humans and other animals are differences of degree, not of kind, because all species descend from common ancestors.
com: If the human body and brain come from a long history shared with other animals, it would be odd for the capacity to feel to have appeared out of nowhere in our species alone. That is why evolutionary continuity is one of the pillars for attributing pain and emotion to other vertebrates, and increasingly to some invertebrates. It doesn't say that all animals feel the same, only that the question has to be answered with evidence, species by species, and not by a line drawn in advance. See Sentience, Animal consciousness and Animal cognition.

def: A rule of method proposed by the British psychologist Conwy Lloyd Morgan in 1894: an animal's behavior should not be explained by a higher mental capacity if it can be explained by a simpler one.
com: For much of the 20th century, the canon was used to deny emotions and thought to animals. Today many scientists point out that the simplest explanation is not always the one that denies a mind: if a dog and a human react to injury in the same way and have similar brain structures, it may be simpler to assume that both feel pain. Morgan himself didn't mean to forbid mental explanations when there is evidence for them. See Anthropomorphism, Evolutionary continuity and Critical anthropomorphism.

def: The conscious and controlled use of our own experience to form hypotheses about what an animal feels or thinks, which are then tested by observation and experiments; an approach associated with the ethologist Gordon Burghardt.
com: It sits between two errors: projecting human feelings onto everything an animal does, and denying any mental life on principle. Critical anthropomorphism takes into account the biology and typical behavior of the species. A dog wagging its tail isn't necessarily happy, but a pig that avoids a place where it felt pain offers a clue that can be tested. See Anthropomorphism, Morgan's canon and Ethology.

pt: Declaração de Cambridge sobre a Consciência
def: A declaration signed by a group of neuroscientists on July 7, 2012, at the University of Cambridge, stating that humans are not the only beings with the neurological substrates that generate consciousness.
com: The text states that all mammals and birds, and many other animals such as octopuses, have these substrates. It is neither a law nor a formal consensus of all of science, but it carried great public weight because it came from researchers in the field. In 2024, the New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness went further, speaking of a realistic possibility of conscious experience in all vertebrates and many invertebrates. See Animal consciousness, Subjective experience and Sentience.

def: Affective states, such as fear, anger, joy, grief or the urge to play, experienced by nonhuman animals and studied by ethology and affective neuroscience.
com: For a long time science avoided talking about emotions in animals, partly because of the legacy of Descartes, who saw animals as machines. Charles Darwin had already devoted a book to the expression of emotions in humans and animals, in 1872. The neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp, who coined the term affective neuroscience, identified basic emotional systems in ancient brain regions that mammals share. Knowing that an animal can feel fear or joy changes the moral question: avoiding physical pain is not enough. See Animal-machine, Positive experiences and Suffering.

def: A view associated with the philosopher René Descartes, in the 17th century, that animals are mindless automata whose cries and movements are merely mechanical reactions, without feeling.
com: This idea helped justify experiments on living animals with no concern for pain, and shaped Western science for centuries. Historians debate how far Descartes himself denied all sensation to animals, but the doctrine associated with him was used in exactly that way. Today it is rejected by biology and neuroscience. See Evolutionary continuity, Animal emotions and Vivisection.

def: Contempt for or aversion to animals and nature, seen as inferior, dirty or cruel; a term coined by the writer Jim Mason in the book *An Unnatural Order* (1993), by analogy with misogyny.
com: It shows up in everyday expressions, such as calling a cruel person an animal or a beast, and in the idea that nature is nothing but violence. Mason argues that this attitude grew with agriculture and animal husbandry, and that it makes exploitation easier: it is easier to use those we despise. See Dominionism, Anthropocentrism and Ecofeminism.

def: The view that humans have the right to rule over and use other animals and nature, often based on the passage in Genesis in which God gives humans dominion over the animals.
com: There are different readings of this passage within the religions themselves. Many theologians, Jewish and Christian, understand dominion as stewardship, that is, a responsibility to care, and not as a license to exploit. The debate shows that faith does not necessarily lead to speciesism. See Theocentrism, Religious speciesism, Anthropocentrism and Misothery.

def: A Greek term for purpose or proper nature; in animal ethics, used by the philosopher Bernard Rollin for the set of needs and interests characteristic of each species, such as a pig's need to root or a hen's need to scratch and dust-bathe.
com: Rollin argued that respecting an animal includes letting it live according to its nature, not only avoiding pain. The idea helps explain why confinement causes suffering even without injuries. Critics point out that genetic engineering can alter the telos itself, for instance by creating animals that tolerate confinement better, which shows the concept needs to be combined with attention to what the individual feels. See Psychological integrity, Animal confinement and Genetic engineering.

def: The tendency to give less consideration to small animals, or to young ones, than to large animals, for example by accepting painful procedures on them that would not be done without anesthesia on a larger animal.
com: It shows up in the castration and tail docking of piglets and lambs without anesthesia, in procedures performed on mice and in the disregard for fish and insects. Body size doesn't say how much an animal feels, and there are indications that young animals can feel pain intensely. It is a form of bias that leads to inconsistent decisions. See Speciesism, Bias and Castration.

def: Treating a sentient being as a thing, resource or product, erasing their status as an individual with interests of their own.
com: Language plays a part: calling animals "units", "head" or "stock", or using "it" instead of "he" or "she", helps us forget that someone is there. That is why part of the movement proposes language that treats animals as subjects. See Commodification, Absent referent and Euphemism.

def: A mild word or expression used in place of a more direct or unpleasant one.
com: Animal use is full of euphemisms: "slaughter" or "processing" instead of killing, "sacrifice" for the killing of animals at the end of experiments, "harvest" for hunting and fishing, "animal protein" instead of the flesh of an animal. They are not necessarily dishonest, but they reduce discomfort and draw attention away from the victim. Pointing this out calmly, without accusing the speaker, helps the conversation. See Objectification, Absent referent and Humane washing.

def: A British law of 1822, proposed by the Irish MP Richard Martin, which prohibited the mistreatment of cattle, horses, sheep and other farm and working animals; it is considered one of the first national animal protection laws.
com: The law did not protect dogs and cats, and animals remained property, but it paved the way for the first animal protection society, in 1824, which later became the RSPCA. It shows that legal protection of animals began with the idea of cruelty, not of rights. See Animal cruelty, Animals as property and Welfarism.

def: A report by a British government committee, published in 1965, on the welfare of animals in intensive farming systems; it was a response to Ruth Harrison's book *Animal Machines* (1964).
com: The report argued that every animal should at least be able to turn around, groom itself, get up, lie down and stretch its limbs, and it recognized that animals can suffer mentally. These ideas gave rise to the Five Freedoms, later formulated by the UK's Farm Animal Welfare Council. It is a landmark in the beginning of animal welfare science. See Five Freedoms, Animal welfare science and Animal confinement.

def: The recognition, in laws and treaties, that animals are sentient beings and not mere things.
com: In the European Union, Article 13 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, in force since the Treaty of Lisbon (2009), requires paying regard to the welfare of animals as sentient beings, but makes exceptions for religious rites, cultural traditions and regional heritage. France began defining animals in its Civil Code as living beings endowed with sensitivity in 2015, and the United Kingdom passed an animal sentience law in 2022. The recognition is a symbolic step forward, but on its own it bans no practice: animals are still treated as property. See Animals as property, Animal legal personhood and Sentience.

def: In Brazil, Law 9,605 of 1998, whose Article 32 makes it a crime to abuse, mistreat, injure or mutilate wild, domestic or domesticated animals, whether native or exotic.
com: The same article punishes anyone who carries out a painful or cruel experiment on a live animal, even for teaching or scientific purposes, when alternative resources exist. In 2020, Law 14,064, known as the Sansão Law, raised the penalty for abusing dogs and cats to two to five years in prison. The difference in penalty between dogs and cats and other animals is an example of institutional speciesism, and the practices of regulated livestock farming are generally not treated as abuse. See Animal cruelty, Institutional speciesism and Animal law.

def: Brazilian Law 11,794 of 2008, which regulates the use of vertebrate animals in scientific research and teaching, created the National Council for the Control of Animal Experimentation (CONCEA) and made Animal Use Ethics Committees mandatory.
com: It is named after the public health doctor and congressman Sérgio Arouca, author of the original bill. The law regulates experimentation rather than banning it: it requires institutions to be accredited, projects to receive ethical approval and attention to alternative methods. Critics argue that it legitimized practices that had been challenged in court, and supporters say it brought rules where there were almost none before. See Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA), Animal experimentation and 3Rs.

pt: Comissão de Ética no Uso de Animais (CEUA)
def: A committee that reviews and approves, or rejects, an institution's research and teaching projects involving animals; in Brazil, mandatory under the Arouca Law, with equivalents in other countries, such as IACUCs in the United States.
com: The committee must check whether the use of animals is justified, whether the number of animals is the minimum needed and whether pain will be controlled. Studies of committees of this kind point to limits: they are generally made up mostly of researchers from the institution itself, and they rarely reject projects. Including outside members, such as representatives of animal protection societies, is one way of balancing this review. See Arouca Law, 3Rs and Animal experimentation.

def: An initiative launched in 1993 by the philosophers Paola Cavalieri and Peter Singer, which calls for extending three basic rights to chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans: to life, to liberty and not to be tortured.
com: The project helped put on the agenda the idea that other animals can have legal rights. Several countries have banned or restricted the use of great apes in research. Sentientists support protecting these animals, but criticize a criterion based on similarity to humans, which can leave out other beings who also feel. See Animals as persons, Animal habeas corpus and Animal legal personhood.

def: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora, a treaty signed in 1973 and in force since 1975, which controls or prohibits trade between countries in threatened species.
com: Species are listed in appendices according to their level of threat, and commercial trade in the most threatened is prohibited. The convention protects species, not individuals: an animal of a common species is not protected by it, and the treaty does not deal with suffering in transport or captivity. Even so, it is the main international tool against the trafficking of wild animals. See Animal trafficking, Extinction and Holistic environmentalism.

def: A body of research that finds an association between animal abuse and other forms of violence, such as domestic violence, child abuse and violent crime.
com: Because of this research, some protection services began cross-reporting animal abuse and domestic violence, and the FBI began recording animal cruelty crimes in their own category from 2016. Overstatement should be avoided: the association is statistical, and most people who mistreat an animal do not go on to commit serious crimes against people. Nor should the argument be the only reason to protect animals, who matter in themselves. See Animal cruelty and Empathy.

pt: Proibição de testes de cosméticos em animais
def: Laws that prohibit testing cosmetics, toiletries and perfumes, or their ingredients, on animals, and in some cases selling products that were tested.
com: The European Union banned testing of finished products in 2004 and completed its ban on selling cosmetics with ingredients tested on animals in 2013. In Brazil, Law 15,183 of 2025 banned the use of live vertebrate animals in tests of cosmetics, personal hygiene products, perfumes and ingredients used only in these products. There are loopholes: ingredients that also have other uses may be tested when other rules, such as chemical safety rules, require it. See Cruelty-free, Replacement methods and Draize test.

pt: Objeção de consciência à experimentação animal
def: The right of students, teachers and professionals to refuse to take part in practices that use or kill animals, such as dissection in classes, without suffering academic or professional harm.
com: Italy has had a law recognizing this right since 1993. In many courses, refusals opened the way to replacement methods, such as models, computer simulations and the bodies of animals that died of natural causes, and comparative studies have found no loss of learning with these methods. See Replacement methods, 3Rs and Vivisection.

def: An animal used in research to represent a biological process or a human disease, such as mice genetically altered to develop a type of cancer.
com: The choice of species often follows the Krogh principle, from the Danish physiologist August Krogh: for each problem there is an animal in which it can be studied most conveniently. Being convenient doesn't guarantee that the result holds for humans. Most drugs that pass preclinical testing fail in human trials, through lack of efficacy or safety problems, and differences between species are one of the causes discussed. Supporters point out that animal models have contributed to medical advances; critics advocate methods based on human biology. In 2022, the United States stopped requiring animal tests for approving new drugs. See Animal experimentation, Replacement methods and 3Rs.

def: The process, over many generations, by which animal populations came to live under human control and were modified by artificial selection; the dog was first, more than 15,000 years ago, and cattle, sheep, goats and pigs were domesticated around 10,000 years ago.
com: Domestication changed bodies and behavior: hens that lay around 300 eggs a year, broiler chickens that grow so fast that many have leg problems, cows with enormous udders. A common argument says these animals exist thanks to us and so we may use them. But having brought someone into existence doesn't give the right to make them suffer. For veganism, ending exploitation doesn't mean releasing domesticated animals, but no longer breeding them for use and caring for those who already exist. See Artificial selection, Domestic animal and Sanctuary.

def: The breeding of animals of wild species in zoos, aquariums or conservation centers, generally with the stated aim of maintaining populations of threatened species.
com: There are success stories with release back into the wild, such as the golden lion tamarin in Brazil and Przewalski's horse in Mongolia. But most animals born in zoos are never released, many belong to species that are not threatened, and surplus animals may be sold or killed. The ethical question is whether the good of the species justifies each individual's life in captivity. See Zoo, Extinction and Holistic environmentalism.

def: A set of methods for reducing the number of animals in a population, ranging from killing (culling, hunting, poisoning) to non-lethal methods such as neutering and contraception.
com: For stray dogs and cats, trap-neuter-return (TNR) is an alternative to capture and killing. In wild animals, contraceptive vaccines are already used, for example in wild horses in the United States. From a sentientist point of view, non-lethal methods are preferable when they work, and the question is not only how many animals there are, but how they live and die. Killing is often defended as cheaper or faster, but in many cases the population grows back. See Castration, Invasive alien species and Pests.

def: A species taken by humans outside its native range that spreads and causes harm to ecosystems, other species or the economy, such as the European wild boar in Brazil.
com: These species are usually fought by large-scale killing, which creates a conflict between the conservationist view, which values species and ecosystems, and the sentientist view, which looks at each individual. The invasive animals themselves are not to blame for being there. Sentientists don't deny the ecological harm, but call for methods that cause less suffering and for attention also to the native animals affected. In Brazil, the boar hunting authorized for control has been criticized for also serving as a pretext for sport hunting. See Holistic environmentalism, Sentientist environmentalism and Animal population control.

def: A metal trap with two jaws that snap shut on an animal's leg and hold it until the trapper arrives; used mainly to catch animals for their fur.
com: The animal may stay trapped for hours or days, with fractures, dehydration and fear, and some chew off their own leg to escape. Non-target animals, including dogs and protected species, are also caught. The European Union approved a ban on these traps in 1991, effective from 1995, but they remain legal in other countries. See Hunting, Fur and leather and Suffering.

def: The keeping of bears, mainly Asiatic black bears, in small cages for the periodic extraction of bile from the gallbladder, used in the traditional medicine of some Asian countries.
com: Extraction is done through catheters or open wounds in the abdomen, and the bears may spend years confined, with pain, infections and stereotypic behaviors. The active substance in bile, ursodeoxycholic acid, can be produced without animals, and there are plant alternatives within traditional medicine itself. The practice remains legal in China. Vietnam banned it in 2005, and South Korea approved the end of bear farming for bile from 2026. See Animal confinement, Stereotypic behavior and Animal trafficking.

def: The ability of bacteria and other microorganisms to survive drugs that used to kill them, which makes infections harder to treat.
com: One of the causes is the mass use of antibiotics in animal farming, often to prevent diseases favored by confinement or to speed up growth. Estimates published in the journal *Science* in 2019 indicate that about three quarters of the antimicrobials sold worldwide are used in farmed animals. The World Health Organization considers resistance one of the greatest threats to global health, and the European Union banned the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in 2006. It is a public health argument that adds to the ethical one. See Industrial livestock farming, Factory farm and Zoonosis.

def: A form of recreational fishing in which the fish is hooked, taken out of the water and returned alive.
com: It is presented as harmless or sustainable, but the hook injures the mouth and sometimes the gills, the struggle and time out of water cause stress, and some fish die after release. Research on pain in fish, such as the biologist Lynne Sneddon's work with trout, shows responses to injury that go beyond reflex. If the fish can feel, injuring them for fun is hard to justify, even when they go back into the water. See Fishing, Pain and Sentience.

def: The use of animals, such as dogs, horses and cats, in health treatment, rehabilitation or education, under professional supervision.
com: There is evidence of benefits for some people, such as reduced anxiety, although many studies are small. The ethical question is the animal's side: they need rest, the ability to refuse contact and not to be exposed to constant stress. Practices such as therapy with captive dolphins are criticized because they depend on capturing or confining animals who suffer in those conditions. See Companion animal, Animal welfare and Animal entertainment.

def: An animal shelter that does not kill healthy or treatable animals for lack of space or adopters, keeping euthanasia for cases of untreatable suffering.
com: In Brazil, Law 14,228 of 2021 prohibited zoonosis control agencies, public kennels and official establishments from killing dogs and cats, except by euthanasia in cases of serious or incurable infectious diseases. No-kill shelters depend on neutering, adoption and intake management, and can become overcrowded when these policies are lacking. See Euthanasia, Adoption and Animal population control.

def: The movement that opposes vivisection and, more broadly, experimentation on animals; organized mainly from the 19th century in the United Kingdom.
com: The Irish writer Frances Power Cobbe founded one of the first antivivisection societies in 1875, and in 1876 the United Kingdom passed the first law regulating experiments on animals. The movement brought together many women and had links with women's suffrage. Today part of it calls for an end to all experimentation and part for gradual replacement by animal-free methods. See Vivisection, Animal experimentation and Replacement methods.

def: The set of bodily and behavioral responses to a threat or challenge, such as the release of hormones like cortisol, a faster heart rate and flight.
com: Short-term stress is part of life and helps an animal react to danger. The problem is intense or prolonged stress, sometimes called distress, when the animal can no longer adapt and their health and behavior deteriorate, as in many confinement systems. Measuring hormones helps but is not enough: cortisol also rises in good situations, such as mating, so scientists combine several indicators. See Coping, Suffering and Stereotypic behavior.

def: An animal's effort, through body and behavior, to deal with the challenges of their environment and keep their physical and mental balance.
com: The welfare scientist Donald Broom defined an individual's welfare as their state as regards their attempts to cope with the environment: the harder or more impossible it is to cope, the worse the welfare. An animal can be coping successfully and still be suffering, and failure to cope leads to disease, stereotypies and helplessness. See Stress, Animal welfare and Learned helplessness.

def: Changes to the environment of captive animals, such as objects, hiding places, material to root in, challenges to obtain food, or company, to encourage natural behaviors and reduce boredom and frustration.
com: Studies show that enrichment can reduce stereotypies and improve the health of animals in zoos, laboratories and farms. But it has limits: a toy in a cramped pen doesn't make up for lack of space, social life or freedom. It can also be used as a showcase to justify captivity. See Stereotypic behavior, Zoo and Humane washing.

def: A model for assessing animal welfare created by the New Zealand scientist David Mellor and colleagues in 1994, which looks at nutrition, physical environment, health and behavioral interactions in order to infer the fifth domain, the animal's mental state.
com: Unlike the Five Freedoms, which focus on avoiding what is bad, the Five Domains also look for positive experiences, such as comfort, play and curiosity. The model was updated in 2020 and is used by several organizations and governments. Even an animal with a good score may be killed young for food, which the model does not assess. See Five Freedoms, Positive experiences and A life worth living.

pt: Vida que vale a pena ser vivida
def: The idea that welfare should not only avoid suffering but ensure that the animal's life, overall, has more good experiences than bad ones; used by the UK's farm animal welfare council since 2009.
com: The concept forces us to ask whether an animal's life has a positive balance, not only whether they were spared some pain. Many intensively farmed animals would hardly pass this test. At the same time, sentientists point out that a good life doesn't justify taking it early: death is also a harm. See Welfare range, Harm of death and Five Domains.

pt: Escala de expressão facial de dor (grimace scale)
def: A method for assessing pain in animals by changes in facial expression, such as narrowed eyes, tightened muzzle and cheeks, and ears and whiskers in a different position.
com: The first scale was published in 2010 for mice, and versions followed for rats, rabbits, horses, sheep, pigs and cats, among others. They show that many animals show pain in their faces, as humans do, and help vets and researchers recognize pain that used to go unnoticed. See Pain, Nociception and Animal behavior.

def: An idealized, highly humanized portrayal of animals in films, cartoons and products, in which they talk, think and feel like people and have adventures without hunger, disease or death.
com: The term comes from the Disney studios' animated films, but it describes a wider phenomenon in popular culture. These stories can stir empathy for animals, but they also give a false picture of how animals live, both in the wild and on farms. There is also a contrast: many children grow up loving cartoon piglets and chickens while eating those same animals. See Anthropomorphism, Critical anthropomorphism and Cognitive dissonance.

def: Teaching that seeks to develop compassion, respect and responsibility toward animals, people and the environment, through activities in schools and communities.
com: It emerged in the late 19th century, linked to the first animal protection societies, which brought to schools the idea that treating animals well shapes kinder people. Today it includes topics such as responsible guardianship, alternatives to using animals in classes and where food comes from. It can stop at welfare or go as far as questioning exploitation, depending on who practices it. See The Link and Companion animal.

def: Producing an animal genetically identical to another, from the genetic material of a body cell of the original animal.
com: The first mammal cloned from an adult cell was Dolly the sheep, born in 1996 at the Roslin Institute in Scotland after hundreds of attempts. The technique still has a low success rate: many embryos fail to develop, and many animals are born with health problems or die young. It is used in research, in animal farming, in conservation programs and, commercially, to "clone" pet dogs and cats, which requires surrogate mothers and many animals undergoing procedures. See Artificial reproduction and Animal model.

def: A relationship of affection and companionship between people and animals, which can bring benefits to both.
com: It is studied mainly with companion animals, and there is research on effects on people's health and well-being, although the results are mixed. The bond shows that many people recognize animals as someone, not something. At the same time, it reveals an arbitrary division: the affection given to dogs and cats rarely extends to pigs, cows and chickens, who have similar capacities. A healthy bond also requires attending to the animal's needs, not only to what they offer people. See Companion animal, Animal-assisted therapy and Cognitive dissonance.

def: Information obtained by observation, measurement, experiment or record that makes a claim more or less likely.
com: Not all evidence weighs the same. In general, personal accounts count less than observational studies, which count less than controlled experiments, and reviews that pool many studies count more than a single study; the consensus of scientific bodies shows where the evidence converges. Having little evidence is not the same as having evidence against. And the demand applies to both sides: animal advocates also need to back their claims about health, the environment and data with evidence. See Fact, Science, Pseudoscience and Evidence-based practice.

def: The absence of contradiction between the statements of an argument or of a set of beliefs.
com: Consistency guarantees internal logic, but not external truth: a set of beliefs can be perfectly consistent and still false, if it starts from a false premise. So, besides consistency, a good argument needs true premises, supported by evidence. In debate, pointing out an inconsistency shows that some belief has to change, but doesn't by itself say which. It differs from moral consistency, which asks us to apply the same principles to similar cases. See Logic, Moral consistency and Evidence.

def: A way of deciding that uses the best available evidence about what works, rather than relying only on intuition, tradition or preference.
com: The idea took hold in medicine in the 1990s, with evidence-based medicine, and spread to other fields such as education and public policy. In animal advocacy, research organizations study which campaigns, messages and strategies reduce suffering the most. It requires humility: evidence about strategies is limited and changes over time. And it doesn't replace ethics: evidence helps choose the means, but the reason to defend animals comes from sentience. See Evidence, Rationalist (or evidence-based) veganism and Effective altruism.

def: A disposition to act for the benefit of others, even when it brings no advantage to the one who acts, or has some cost.
com: The term was coined in the 19th century by the philosopher Auguste Comte, as the opposite of egoism. In biology, it also describes animal behavior that helps others, such as warning the group about a predator. In animal ethics, altruism shows up when someone changes habits or devotes time and resources to beings who will never repay them. But the defense of animals doesn't depend on altruism: not causing avoidable harm is a duty, not a generous gesture. See Effective altruism, Egoism (egocentrism), Charity and Compassion.

def: An attitude of putting one's own interests first, without considering, or barely considering, the interests of others.
com: In everyday use, egoism and egocentrism blur together, but they aren't the same: in psychology, egocentrism is difficulty seeing things from other people's point of view, common in young children, and not a moral choice. In philosophy, psychological egoism says people always act out of self-interest, and ethical egoism says they ought to; the guide discusses the latter on its page about egoism and Objectivism. The argument "I like it, so I eat it" puts one's own pleasure above another being's life. See Altruism, Speciesism and Anthropocentrism.

def: Help given voluntarily to those in need, such as donations of money, time or goods, usually without expecting anything in return.
com: In the animal cause, charity shows up in donations to shelters, sanctuaries and organizations, and in rescues. It is valuable, but there is an important critique: treating animals as objects of charity, rather than as beings with rights, suggests that helping them is an optional favor. For many animal advocates, what animals need is justice, starting with not being exploited. Charity can also be more or less effective, and some organizations assess where donations reduce the most suffering. See Altruism, Effective altruism and Rights.

def: The activity of organized groups that seek to influence laws, public policies and government decisions in favor of their interests; also the group that exerts this pressure.
com: The word comes from the lobbies where legislators were approached. Lobbying is legal and common in democracies, but each group's power is very unequal. In Brazil, the farming sector has one of the largest parliamentary caucuses in Congress, and it tends to weigh in on issues such as environmental licensing and animal welfare rules. Animal protection organizations also lobby, for example for bans on cosmetics testing on animals. See Lobbying, Agribusiness and Representation.

def: The practice or system of lobbies and lobbyists acting on those who decide public policy.
com: Whether the activity should have its own transparency rules, such as registering lobbyists and disclosing meetings, has been debated for years, to reduce the risk of undue influence. See Lobby.

def: Measures, usually temporary, that seek to correct historical inequalities affecting discriminated groups, giving them more access to opportunities.
com: The best-known example in Brazil is quotas in public universities, which the Supreme Federal Court ruled constitutional in 2012 and which became mandatory in federal universities by law that same year. The underlying idea is that treating equally those who start from very unequal situations can keep the inequality in place. This connects with the principle of equal consideration of interests: equal consideration doesn't mean identical treatment, but giving the same weight to what each one needs. See Intersectionality, Representation and Equal consideration.

def: The presence of people from different social groups in spaces of decision-making, visibility and voice, such as governments, companies, media and social movements.
com: A movement with broader representation tends to hear more experiences and reach more people; in the animal movement, there are criticisms that in some countries it is still dominated by certain social groups. There is also an issue specific to the cause: animals can't represent themselves or vote, and depend on humans to defend their interests. That is why there are proposals for the political representation of animals, and parties devoted to them, such as the Party for the Animals in the Netherlands, which first won seats in parliament in 2006. See Lobby, Affirmative action and Intersectionality.

def: Public resources given to a sector or product, such as direct payments, cheap credit, insurance or price guarantees, to lower its costs or sustain its production.
com: According to a 2021 report by FAO, UNDP and UNEP, support to agricultural producers worldwide amounts to about 540 billion dollars a year, and 87% of it distorts prices or causes environmental and social harm. Much of it goes to animal farming and feed grains, which helps keep meat, milk and eggs artificially cheap. The environmentalist critique asks for prices to include costs to the environment and health, but the animal-centered critique goes further: the gravest cost, the suffering and death of animals, isn't counted at all. And a caution: a policy that charged only for environmental impact could make chicken and fish cheaper, since they emit less per kilo, and increase the number of animals killed. Well-justified subsidies would be those supporting plant proteins, fermentation and cultivated meat. See Tax incentive, Agribusiness and Externality.

def: A reduction of or exemption from taxes granted by the government to encourage an activity, a sector or the consumption of a product.
com: Tax incentives usually apply to products considered essential or strategic. In Brazil's tax reform, for example, meats were included in the national basic food basket with a zero tax rate, alongside foods such as rice and beans. From the animals' point of view, the problem is that the tax doesn't account for the cost production imposes on them: a product that requires confining, causing suffering to and killing sentient beings gets the same treatment as, or better than, alternatives that don't. Being strategic or profitable for the economy doesn't make a practice just. A tax policy that took animals seriously would favor plant proteins and new food technologies, not exploitation. See Subsidies and Externality.

def: A cost or benefit that an activity causes to other people, or other beings, and that doesn't show up in the product's price.
com: In the production of meat, milk and eggs, the most cited externalities are water and air pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, deforestation, antibiotic resistance and the risk of new diseases from animals. Since these costs aren't in the price, society pays them, and the product seems cheaper than it is. The animal-centered critique adds a point usually left out even of this account: the suffering and death of the animals themselves, which aren't even treated as a cost, because the animals are seen as the product. See Subsidies, Tax incentive and Antimicrobial resistance.

def: The power of a state, court or authority to apply the law and settle disputes; also the territory or subject matter over which that power applies.
com: Animal protection varies greatly from one jurisdiction to another: a practice banned in one country may be allowed next door, and companies sometimes move abroad what is banned at home. That's why animal advocacy happens at several levels at once: municipal, state, national and international. See Statute, Law and Animal protection legislation.

def: A written, general and binding rule passed by the legislature through the process set out in the constitution.
com: Statutes sit within a hierarchy: below the constitution and above decrees and regulations. In Brazil, the Constitution itself prohibits practices that subject animals to cruelty (art. 225), and laws such as the Environmental Crimes Law and the Arouca Law deal with cruelty and the use of animals in research. A statute can protect animals or allow their exploitation, and something being legal doesn't settle whether it is just. See Law, Jurisdiction and Animal protection legislation.

def: The body of laws and rules that protect animals against cruelty and regulate their use, in areas such as farming, transport, slaughter, research and entertainment.
com: Most of this legislation is welfarist: it limits how animals are used, but doesn't ban using them. Some rules go further and recognize animals as sentient beings, such as the Treaty of Lisbon in the European Union. See Animal law, Statute, Sentience in law and Welfarism.

def: Rights that non-human animals would have, in the moral or legal sense, such as not being killed, confined or used as property.
com: The theory of animal rights took shape with the philosopher Tom Regan, in *The Case for Animal Rights* (1983), for whom animals who are subjects-of-a-life have intrinsic value and cannot be treated as mere resources. It differs from welfarism, which accepts using animals as long as suffering is reduced. Not to be confused with animal law, the branch of law that studies rules about animals: one thing is the field of study, another is the thesis that animals have rights. See Animal law, Rights, Intrinsic value and Abolitionism.

def: The branch of philosophy that studies what is right and wrong, good and bad, and how we should act; in practice, another name for ethics.
com: It is usually divided into three parts: metaethics, which asks what moral judgments are and whether they can be true; normative ethics, which proposes criteria for what we should do, such as utilitarianism, deontology and virtue ethics; and applied ethics, which discusses concrete cases, such as abortion, the death penalty and the use of animals. Animal ethics is part of applied ethics, but depends on the other two. See Ethics, Normative ethics and Animal ethics.

def: The branch of philosophy that studies the nature of the mind and consciousness, and the relationship between the mind and the body, or the brain.
com: Some of its central questions lie at the heart of the debate about animals: how we know other beings have minds, the so-called problem of other minds; what it is to have an experience, Thomas Nagel's question of "what it is like to be a bat" (1974); and why physical processes give rise to experiences, the "hard problem of consciousness", as David Chalmers called it (1995). The same questions come back in the discussion of whether AIs and robots could come to feel. See Consciousness, Subjective experience, Epistemology and Sentience in AI and digital systems.

def: Extreme or rare situations at the boundary of a rule, such as the desert island with no other food or the choice between saving a dog and a child.
com: Used well, they test whether a principle holds in every case or needs adjusting, and show where a rule's limits lie. The argument from marginal cases, for example, uses humans with limited capacities to test whether rationality is really the criterion for moral consideration. Used badly, they turn the exception into the rule: from the fact that someone would eat an animal on a desert island it doesn't follow that they may buy one at the supermarket, where there is no necessity at all. The useful question about an edge case is: what does it show about the ordinary case? See Hypothetical scenarios and Argument from marginal cases.

def: Imagined situations used to test ideas and principles; when built for this purpose in philosophy, they are called thought experiments.
com: They are used on both sides of the debate, and can help or hinder. They help when they isolate what matters morally: vegans ask, for example, whether extraterrestrials more intelligent than us could breed and eat us, to test whether intelligence justifies exploiting those who are less intelligent; or whether an AI that felt pain would deserve consideration, to test whether the criterion is sentience rather than species or the material a being is made of. They hinder when the scenario is impossible or poorly described and hides premises, when an intuition about an artificial case is treated as proof, or when it serves to dodge the real decision, as in "what if they discover plants feel?" faced with a choice made today. This also applies to animal advocates: an analogy with extraterrestrials that ignores relevant differences is unconvincing. See Edge cases, Sentience in extraterrestrial life, Sentience in AI and digital systems and Logical consistency.

def: A vegan who rejects animal exploitation but still gives less weight to the interests of some sentient beings just because of their species.
com: Veganism starts from the principle of not exploiting animals. Antispeciesism goes further: it asks that similar interests of any sentient being weigh equally, whatever the species, including in situations that don't involve exploitation. A vegan can be speciesist in two ways. The first is discriminating among animals by species without justification, such as caring about dogs, cows and dolphins while dismissing fish, insects and other invertebrates who may also feel, which the glossary calls xenospeciesism. The second is ignoring sentient beings in scenarios beyond exploitation: wild animal suffering, treated as "just nature" even when helping would be possible; animals seen as pests, killed without need or in cruel ways; animals hit by disasters, road traffic or pollution, who get attention only when they belong to favored species. Dismissing possible new minds, such as sentient AIs, in advance is a similar mistake, but it isn't speciesism, because they belong to no species: the name for that bias is substratism, or carbonism when it favors organic bodies. The critique works as self-criticism, to carry the principle all the way through, not to invalidate veganism: pointing out that some vegans are speciesist doesn't show that exploiting animals is acceptable. See Speciesism, Xenospeciesism, Antispeciesism, Wild animal suffering and Substratism.

def: The field that studies the nutritional needs of non-human animals and how to meet them through feeding.
com: In animal farming, it focuses on making animals grow and produce more at the lowest cost, measuring feed conversion, how much feed becomes meat, milk or eggs. This conversion reveals an inefficiency: the animal spends most of what it eats on living, and only part becomes food for people. The same field also serves welfare, when it looks after the health of companion, rescued and sanctuary animals, and it is the field that studies whether foods without animal ingredients meet the needs of dogs and cats. See Nutrition, Feed, Vegan pet food and Zootechnics (animal science).

def: The study of the mind and behavior of non-human animals, such as perception, learning, memory, emotions and social relationships; also called comparative psychology.
com: For a long time the field was shaped by behaviorism, which studied only observable behavior and avoided talk of mind, often with experiments that caused suffering, such as the learned helplessness experiments on dogs. Today, together with ethology and the science of animal cognition, it provides much of the evidence that many animals feel fear, pleasure and stress, learn, and have complex social lives. There is also an applied side, which deals with behavior problems in companion and captive animals. Not to be confused with the psychology that studies humans' relationship with animals, such as the meat paradox. See Animal cognition, Ethology, Animal emotions and Morgan's canon.

def: A person who follows veganism, that is, who seeks to exclude, as far as is possible and practicable, all forms of exploitation of and cruelty to animals, in food, clothing, entertainment and other uses; also the adjective for products and practices free of animal origin or exploitation.
com: The word was coined in 1944 by Donald Watson and other founders of the Vegan Society, in England, from the first and last letters of "vegetarian". Being vegan isn't just a diet: someone who eats only plants but wears leather or pays to watch animals in shows follows a vegan diet without being vegan. The phrase "as far as is possible and practicable" acknowledges that living without causing any harm to animals is impossible; the commitment is to avoid what can be avoided. See Veganism, Vegan diet, Vegetarian and Speciesist vegan.

def: A person who doesn't eat the meat of any animal, including fish and seafood; in the most common sense, they may consume other animal products, such as milk, eggs and honey.
com: Many people call someone who eats fish or chicken a vegetarian, but that usage is wrong: someone who eats fish is a pescetarian. Most vegetarians are lacto-ovo vegetarians. That is the broad and most common sense; in the strict sense, a vegetarian is someone who consumes no animal products in their diet, which in Brazil is called a strict vegetarian. It's worth noting that, in most of the industry, producing milk and eggs also involves killing animals, such as the calves separated from cows and the male chicks culled at hatching; so vegetarianism reduces, but doesn't eliminate, participation in the killing. See Vegetarianism, Lacto-ovo vegetarianism, Vegan and Reducetarianism.

def: A person who holds sentientism, that is, who takes sentience, rather than species, substrate or intelligence, as the criterion for moral consideration.
com: For a sentientist, every being able to feel, to have good and bad experiences, deserves to have their interests taken into account, whether a human, another animal or, if one ever exists, a sentient artificial mind. Since the late 2010s, the term has also named a worldview that joins reason and evidence with compassion for all sentient beings. A sentientist isn't necessarily vegan, and a vegan isn't necessarily a sentientist: one starts from a criterion of moral consideration, the other from a commitment not to exploit animals, and the two usually go together. See Sentientism, Sentience, Antispeciesism and Substratism.

def: An expert in ethics: a person who studies, teaches or researches ethics, or who advises institutions on moral questions.
com: Being an ethicist means knowing about ethics, not a guarantee of acting better. The philosophers Eric Schwitzgebel and Joshua Rust compared ethics professors with other professors in the United States and, in a study published in 2014, found that ethicists more often condemned eating the meat of mammals, but didn't report eating less meat than other philosophers. The result shows the gap between knowing and doing, which is why moral consistency is a challenge for everyone, animal advocates included. See Ethics, Animal ethics, Bioethicist and Moral consistency.

def: An expert in bioethics: a person who studies the moral problems of medicine, scientific research and biotechnology, and who often sits on committees that review research and clinical decisions.
com: Bioethicists serve on ethics committees in hospitals and in human research and, in the case of animals, on committees such as Brazil's CEUAs, which review the use of animals in teaching and research. Most of this work follows the 3Rs principle, replacing, reducing and refining the use of animals, which limits harm without questioning whether the use is just. Some bioethicists go further: Peter Singer, one of the central figures of animal ethics, was for decades a professor of bioethics at Princeton University. See Bioethics, Ethicist, 3Rs, Animal Use Ethics Committee (CEUA) and Animal experimentation.

def: An intellectual movement that advocates using science and technology to overcome biological limits, such as ageing, disease, cognitive limitations and suffering.
com: The term was popularized by the biologist Julian Huxley in 1957, and the movement organized in the late 1990s, when Nick Bostrom and David Pearce founded the World Transhumanist Association, now Humanity+. The Transhumanist Declaration advocates the well-being of all sentience, including humans, non-human animals and possible artificial intelligences. Pearce goes further and proposes using technology to abolish suffering in all sentient beings, wild animals included. Not every transhumanist thinks this way: many focus only on enhancing humans. The movement also draws criticism, about unequal access to technologies, the risk of new forms of eugenics and speculative promises; the political scientist Francis Fukuyama went as far as calling it "the world's most dangerous idea". See Transhumanist, Wild animal suffering, Cultivated meat and Sentience in AI and digital systems.

def: A person who holds transhumanism, that is, who advocates using science and technology to overcome the biological limits of humans and, in some versions, of all sentient beings.
com: For the animal cause, the difference between versions matters: a transhumanist focused only on humans can be as speciesist as anyone else, while a sentientist transhumanist sees technology as a means of reducing everyone's suffering, for example through cultivated meat or interventions to help wild animals. See Transhumanism, Sentientist and Wild animal suffering.

def: A person who, knowingly or not, follows carnism, that is, who eats animals because they consider it normal, natural and necessary; also the adjective for what reflects or sustains carnism, such as an advertisement or a policy.
com: The word describes a position, not an insult, and hardly anyone calls themselves a carnist: most people have never thought of eating meat as a choice, which is exactly what the concept points out. So using it in a conversation can sound like an accusation and push the other person away; it usually works better to explain an idea than to label someone. Not every carnist is anti-vegan: many people eat meat and respect, or even admire, those who don't. See Carnism, Non-vegan and Anti-vegan.

def: A person who opposes veganism, often actively; also the adjective for what goes against veganism, such as a speech, a campaign, a law or a joke.
com: Not to be confused with non-vegan: someone who isn't vegan isn't anti-vegan for that reason. An anti-vegan is someone who rejects veganism, mocks vegans or works against the cause, for example with campaigns to restrict vegan products. The hostility is measurable: in a 2017 study, the psychologists Cara MacInnis and Gordon Hodson found that vegans were rated as negatively as, or more negatively than, several other social groups. This guide treats anti-vegan arguments in their strongest version, with what they get right and where they fail, because answering those who disagree well is more useful than dismissing them. See Anti-veganism, Non-vegan and Carnist.

def: A person who isn't vegan; also the adjective for products and practices that involve exploitation or ingredients of animal origin.
com: It is a neutral term, which describes without judging: most people are non-vegan, including vegetarians, reducetarians and those who have never thought about it. Non-vegan isn't a synonym for anti-vegan: it describes what a person consumes, not what they think of veganism. As an adjective, it appears on labels and menus to warn that a product contains milk, eggs, honey, gelatin or other ingredients of animal origin. See Vegan, Anti-vegan and Carnist.

def: A diet that provides the nutrients and energy the body needs and helps prevent disease, based on varied and minimally processed foods.
com: The World Health Organization recommends basing one's diet on fruit, vegetables, legumes, nuts and whole grains, with at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day, and limiting free sugars, saturated fats, trans fats and salt. The 2014 Dietary Guidelines for the Brazilian Population propose a simple rule: make fresh or minimally processed foods the basis of the diet and avoid ultra-processed ones. A well-planned vegan diet can be healthy, with vitamin B12 supplementation, according to bodies such as the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics; but being vegan doesn't make it healthy by itself, because soft drinks and crisps are vegan too. Health and ethics are different questions: the moral question is whether it's necessary to exploit animals to eat well, and the answer of the main nutrition bodies is that it isn't. See Diet, Vegan diet, Nutrition and Evidence.

def: Treating someone merely as a means to others' ends, ignoring their own interests; also using a cause or a person for ends foreign to it.
com: The idea comes from Immanuel Kant, for whom people must always be treated also as ends, and never merely as means. Using someone as a means isn't always wrong: when we buy bread, the baker serves us, but consents and is paid. The problem is using someone merely as a means, without consent and against their interests. Kant didn't extend this principle to animals, but philosophers such as Tom Regan argued that every subject-of-a-life has value of their own and can't be treated as a mere resource. That is what happens in animal farming, where the animal's whole life is organized around what they produce. In the political sense, people also speak of instrumentalizing a cause, for example when animal protection is used only to attack the practices of minority groups, while those of the majority are left out. See Instrumental value, Intrinsic value, Objectification and Subjects-of-a-life.

def: A situation in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief.
com: The term was chosen as word of the year for 2016 by Oxford Dictionaries, the year of the Brexit referendum and the US presidential election. It isn't the same as fake news: fake news is the content, and post-truth is the climate in which it circulates and convinces, because it confirms what people already want to believe. In the debate about animals, it appears on both sides: in advertisements of happy cows that don't show the reality of farms, in nutrition myths that spread on social media, and also in exaggerations by animal advocates. The antidote is the same for everyone: verifiable sources, attention to what scientific bodies say, including where they disagree, and willingness to admit uncertainty. See Truth, Evidence and Cognitive dissonance.

def: The set of companies and activities that breed, slaughter, process and sell animals as meat, from genetics and feed to meatpacking plants, distribution and advertising.
com: It is one of the largest industries in the world: according to FAO data, more than 80 billion land animals are slaughtered each year for consumption, not counting fish, which are measured in tonnes. The sector is concentrated in a few companies, and one of them, Brazil's JBS, is the largest meat processor in the world; Brazil is also the largest exporter of beef and chicken. To protect its prices and image, the industry relies on lobbying, subsidies and advertising with happy animals, fights in court over the use of names like "burger" for plant-based products and, in the United States, backed laws that punish those who secretly film farms, several of which courts have struck down. The costs it doesn't pay fall on others: cattle ranching is the main driver of deforestation in the Amazon, and meatpacking workers face high rates of injury and psychological distress. Criticizing the industry isn't accusing each worker or small producer, who often have few alternatives. See Livestock industry, Industrial livestock farming, Lobby, Subsidies and Externality.

def: What leaves a being worse off than they would otherwise be; in the moral sense, a setback to someone's interests.
